7.3 — Ladders I: The Climbing State

Go and look for a ladder. Search the project for a sprite, a tile, a prefab, an animation clip — search the word itself. The word finds nothing, and that is the trap: there is no ladder prefab, no climb animation and no Ladder tag anywhere in this project, and there is ladder art, sliced into the cave tileset and filed under a number. So the ladder splits in two, and only half of it is art: a look you paint from tiles you already know how to paint (7.1), and a mechanic — a state in which your character is allowed to ignore gravity. The mechanic is the real work.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I climb a ladder?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

Make the character climb. A ladder is not a thing you collide with — it is a place where the normal rules stop applying for a while. So the whole feature is: build a volume that knows you are inside it, let that knowledge change what gravity and your input mean, and then put everything back exactly as it was the moment you step off.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Cut a zone the trigger can seewhat does this part do?Read: the trigger-versus-collision split from 2.1, and the tag ritual you performed on the potion in 2.3
  2. Turn the zone's two messages into one flagwhat does this part do?Read: the coin's OnTriggerEnter2D in 2.1, and the bool you declared for the first time in 5.1
  3. Take gravity away while the flag is upwhat does this part do?Read: the gravityScale branch in 6.3, and the rb.gravityScale row of the Unity + C# Quick Reference
  4. Read the vertical stick and ignore the sideways onewhat does this part do?Read: the movement method you settled on in 2.2, and the input axes from 1.4
  5. Decide which gravity rule gets to winwhat does this part do?Read: the FixedUpdate() gravity branch in 6.3, and the frame-versus-physics-step split from 1.3

The split is not five equal problems. Four of them are shapes you have already typed: a trigger that reports a tagged object (2.1), a bool that remembers something (5.1), a movement line that writes linearVelocity (2.2), and a gravity branch (6.3). Only one idea here is new, and it is the reason the lesson exists. Until today every value in your script described how much — a speed, a force, a fall multiplier. The climb flag describes which rules apply, and it changes the meaning of two numbers you already own without touching either of them. That is what a state is, and it is why the last part of the split is an argument about order rather than a line of code.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the player climb a ladder" cannot be looked up. "Set gravityScale to zero while a bool is true" can — and the page you land on also tells you which body type it applies to, and what a Static body does with the number instead. If a part is small enough to search for, the split is finished.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

Name the single number the climb and the fall-speed rule both want to own, and say which piece of code is allowed to write it last. Then say what the player actually sees when you get that order wrong.

The climb throws the sideways input away. Name a moment in your own level where that would be the wrong call, and say what the player would feel instead.

Your jump uses an impulse — one flick of force — and the climb writes a velocity. Say why an impulse is the wrong tool on a ladder: what would holding W do to a character you flicked upward sixty times a second?

The Problem: A Ladder Nobody Can Find ~15 min

Confirm the situation before you design around it. In the Project window, search ladder, and search climb. Look in Assets/Artwork/Character/Player/ and under the cave tileset. Then open the Player's Animator controller and read its states. You are checking four things, and the answer to the first one is the reason this page has a trap in it at all:

What you might expect to findWhat is actually there
A ladder sprite or tile It is there, and it is numbered. Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/MainLev2.0.png is sliced into 1,829 tiles called MainLev2.0_0 through MainLev2.0_1828, so the word "ladder" is printed on none of them and a search for it finds nothing. The rung column is MainLev2.0_1375 (the head) with _1422, _1468 and _1514 below it, hanging from a beam. This is 7.1's lesson in one search: the art exists, the name does not.
A ladder prefab Nothing. The prefabs are the Player, Coin, Spikes, Axe Item, Switch, Turret, Turret Projectile and Mobile Enemy.
Climb frames on the character Nothing. The Player's controller holds exactly three motions — Idle, Walk and Shovel_Swing — each in Up, Horizontal and Down variants. There is no climb state, and no climbing poses in any of the character sheets.
A "Ladder" tag Nothing. The project's tags are Coin, Enemy, Axe, Spikes, Ground and GroundCheck.
Half the look is already in your tray. Open the Caves palette you loaded in 7.1 and look at what it already holds: the ladder's head tile is in it, and so is the beam it hangs from. The three rung tiles are not — they are sliced and waiting in Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/CavesTileSet/ for you to drag into the tray, which is exactly the move 7.1 taught you. So the look costs one drag and one paint stroke. Remember that number when you are an hour into the mechanic.

So the ladder is yours to build, and it splits cleanly in two. The look is a painting problem, and you have a tileset. The mechanic is the part that has never existed in this project: a state your player can be in that is neither walking nor falling, entered only because a trigger said so.

Movement stateGravityWhich input drives itWhat it looks like
Top-down (Overworld, 5.3) None — the world has no down WASD, four directions The Walk states, driven by WalkDir
Grounded (Platformer, 6.1) Tuned with gravityScale A/D sideways, Space to jump Idle or Walk, driven by IsWalking
Climbing (new today) None — the ladder owns gravity W/S only; sideways is ignored Whatever you decide — see 7.4. For now, a held pose is honest.
Airborne (6.2, 6.3) Tuned, with the fall multiplier Limited — mostly your own momentum Nothing dedicated; the character just moves
Why a held pose is an acceptable first ladder. You cannot animate a climb yet — there are no frames to animate with, and inventing frames is art work, not today's work. A ladder whose character simply holds a standing pose while rising is a complete, shippable mechanic. In 7.4 you will read exactly what adding a real climb animation would involve, and you can decide then whether it is worth it. Nothing about today's build depends on it.

Socratic: What Kind of Thing Is a Ladder?

  1. The ladder has art, but no prefab, no climb animation and no tag. Which of those four is a painting job and which one is the engineering — and why does the art being nearly free not make today easy?
  2. The trigger zone sets a flag on entry and clears it on exit. Compare that with the lever from 5.2, which flips a value and keeps it forever. Why is a ladder remembered only while you are inside it, and a lever remembered permanently? What does each one assume about the player's intent?
  3. Climbing turns gravity off. Your character also had gravity set to zero in the Overworld, in 5.3. The same number means two different things in two different scenes. Say what each one means, and why "gravity zero" is not a fact about the world but a fact about the state.
  4. Your jump uses an impulse (a flick, not a push), and gravity was tuned in 6.1 to make the arc feel right. If the climb sets gravityScale to zero and then restores it, what is the danger of restoring it to a number you typed, rather than to the number you saved in 6.3?
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

Every one of these is a machine that changes what gravity means for the person inside it. Read each for what it does in isolation, then work out which piece of your ladder it is.

Example 1 — A mine-shaft cage's brake, in a hoist controller:

// On the cable the cage is weightless to itself. Off it, it
// carries its full weight again.
brakeForce = onCable ? 0f : fullWeight;

Example 2 — A submarine hatch's interlock, remembering who is inside it:

private bool insideHatch;   // written ONLY by the hatch mouth

Example 3 — A fire-escape's direction lock on a stairwell controller:

// The same vertical stick that walks a landing climbs a ladder.
// One input, two meanings, chosen by where you are standing.

Example 4 — A chairlift's load gate (comment only):

// The gate reports "loaded" for as long as a skier is in the
// gate. It never remembers you after you have moved on.

Example 5 — A rock climber's belay device (comment only):

// The rope holds the climber, not the wall. Let go of the rope
// and the wall does nothing at all.
Architectural specification: the ladder zone. Before you build it, answer every one of these in writing. This is the entire design — the code afterwards is transcription.
  • What shape is the zone, and how tall is it? Should one tall box cover the whole strip, or should you place one box per rung? What does each choice do to the number of enter and exit messages per climb?
  • What does the zone carry that lets your script recognise it? Do you need a new tag, or can you reuse one of the six that exist? If you make a new one, name it exactly.
  • Which two messages does the zone send, and what is the type of the parameter each one hands you?
  • Is the zone a trigger or a solid? What happens to the player if you forget that checkbox — and would you have any error message to tell you?
  • Which single field on the player does the zone write? Name it, and name every place in the project that reads it. A flag read by nobody is decoration.
  • The zone is invisible. What is the player actually looking at when they decide to climb?
Architectural specification: the climb state.
  • While climbing, which input axis is read, and which directions must be ignored? What happens if you leave sideways input live while on a ladder?
  • What is climbSpeed, what type is it, and how is it exposed as a tuning knob? Why does it want to be slower than your walk speed?
  • Which component's gravity is switched off, and to what value? Where does the number come from when you switch it back on — a literal you type, or a value you cached in 6.3? Justify your answer.
  • 6.3 already assigns gravityScale on the physics clock — once per physics step, in FixedUpdate(), from your vertical velocity. If your climb branch sets it to zero in Update() and 6.3's branch then sets it back, which one wins? Predict, test, and describe the symptom the player would see.
  • Your platformer movement is the one you settled on in 2.2 — linearVelocity on a Dynamic body, not transform.Translate. What does that method need in order to move the player straight up a ladder, and why does the ladder's velocity line carry no Time.deltaTime? Then check it against 6.1: a Kinematic body would have ignored your jump impulse entirely, so which body type is on your Player right now?
  • What exits the climb state? List every exit you can think of: reaching the top, jumping, dying, leaving the zone. Which of them happen through the trigger, and which need handling by hand?
Build Lab: Invent the Ladder ~30 min

Step 1 — paint the look. Open the Caves palette from 7.1 and drag the three rung tiles into it from Assets/Artwork/Platformer/Sliced/CavesTileSet/: MainLev2.0_1422, _1468 and _1514. The head, MainLev2.0_1375, is already in the tray — put it on top and you have a four-tile ladder. Paint it one tile wide and let it run from open floor at the bottom up to a ledge at the top. If you would rather invent your own ladder out of the vine or the fractured-rock tiles, do that instead: the mechanic below does not care what the picture is, which is exactly why the picture is the small half of this problem.

Step 2 — decide where the picture lives, and defend it. This is a real design decision, so read all three options before choosing:

Where you paint itWhat happens when you climbThe cost
On No Collision, the picture-only tilemap The player passes cleanly through the strip and rises the whole height. Simplest possible interaction. The ladder is not a solid thing at all — the player can also walk through it sideways at the bottom.
On a new tilemap child (renderer only, no collider), so the ladder pictures are grouped and can be found later Same as above, but the ladder art is a named object you can select, move and reuse. One more tilemap to keep track of, and you must remember it has no collider.
On Collision, the solid tilemap, with the zone in front of it The player is stopped by their own ladder and cannot climb it at all. Fatal as described — unless you leave a one-tile channel beside it, which changes the level.

Step 3 — the zone. Place an empty GameObject at the strip, give it a Box Collider 2D with Is Trigger ticked, and size it to the strip's height. Give it a Ladder tag — create the tag in Project Settings → Tags and Layers, using the same ritual you used for the potion in 2.3. Name the object something you would want to find in three weeks.

Step 4 — the state. Add your flag and your speed knob to PlayerController, and write the two callbacks the zone sends. This is the smallest script in the unit — four lines of behaviour — and the whole difficulty is in the else branch, which is where you restore gravity. Do that first, before you write any climbing movement, and test it: walk into the zone and confirm the flag flips. Print it with Debug.Log while you test. The HUD you built in 5.3 lives in Start and reads only the player's stats — it is not in this scene and it has never heard of a ladder, so a climbing experiment still reports through the Console.

Step 5 — the movement. In Update, inside the branch that only runs in the Platformer scene, add a climbing lane: gravity off, vertical input read, sideways ignored, and the movement done by the method you chose in 2.2. Press Play and climb. Then let go and watch what happens — and be honest about whether the result is what you intended.

The bug you are about to create, and the two ways out. Jump off the ladder while your body is still inside the trigger. You clear the flag by hand so you can jump — but you never left the zone, so the zone never sends its exit message. Land, step back on, and nothing happens: the ladder has gone dead precisely where it used to work. There are two standard repairs, and you should pick one and justify it:
  • A cooldown. When you leave the ladder deliberately, ignore the zone for a fraction of a second. Simple, and it also stops a jump from instantly re-grabbing the ladder on the way up.
  • Trust only the zone. Never set the flag by hand; let the zone's exit message be the only thing that clears it, and gate the jump on isOnLadder && jumpPressed instead. Cleaner in principle, and it makes the jump feel one frame late.
Whichever you choose, write down what the player feels in each case.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name the four tiles a ladder is cut from, and explain why searching the project for "ladder" finds none of them
  • Say which of the ladder's tiles were already on the Caves palette and which you dragged into it yourself
  • Build a trigger zone with its own tag, and explain why it must be a trigger
  • Explain climb as a state: gravity off, vertical input only, and a deliberate restore
  • Say which of the two gravity conflicts — 6.3's physics-step assignment in FixedUpdate() and your climb branch — wins in your build, and how you know
  • Demonstrate the jump-off re-entry bug and defend the repair you chose
  • Explain one input axis serving three meanings, chosen by state
  • Commit and push
